imperial.name: Cucumber, Greenhouse

actions.text:
Sow indoors

Heated glass late Feb–early Mar. Unheated house late Apr.

Plant under glass

Late Mar with reliable heat. Late May in an unheated house once warm.

methods.text:
Sow indoors 

Sow one seed on edge in a 4 in. pot at about 70°F. Water as the compost begins to dry. Protect the fragile roots when moving the seedling on.

Plant in the greenhouse 

Set well-rooted plants into pots, growbags or prepared mounds once the house stays warm. Water in gently and keep water off the stem base.

Prepare a mound 

For the traditional bed method, prepare a compost-rich station about 6 in. deep and 1 ft wide.

Cucumber, Greenhouse.
DIFFICULTY
Tricky
4/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer

Greenhouse cucumbers can produce fruit almost daily in hot weather. They like steady warmth and moist air, but cold, wet compost damages their roots. Train the brittle stems up strings or canes. Check the packet before removing male flowers.

Quick facts
Harvest

Jun – Aug

Germination

3–5 days

Sowing depth

1/2–3/4 in.

Yield per plant

25 cucumbers

Ready in

About 12 weeks from sowing

Heated glass late Feb–early Mar. Unheated house late Apr.

Plant under glass

Late Mar with reliable heat. Late May in an unheated house once warm.

Plant spacing

1 per pot at least 12 in. wide/deep; 2 per growbag; 2 ft between mounds

ALL FEMALE

ALL FEMALE
Mini Munch F1

A greenhouse cucumber with small snack-sized fruits. Pick regularly to encourage a steady supply of young cucumbers.

ORDINARY
Telegraph Improved

A traditional long greenhouse cucumber. Follow variety-specific flower-management advice rather than treating it as an all-female hybrid.

Key risks
Red spider mite

Speckled, yellowing leaves and fine webbing underneath can indicate red spider mite.

Bitterness

Stress, including uneven moisture or temperature, can increase bitterness.

Mildew

Powdery mildew often appears on older leaves later in the season.

Lack of warmth

Cold sowing or planting conditions check growth and can give slugs, woodlice and soil diseases a chance to damage young plants.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
48
FRUITING CROPS

Keep roots warm and evenly moist.

Cold, wet compost checks young plants; avoid both drought and waterlogging.

Check the variety’s flower instructions.

Greenhouse types grown without pollination need any male flowers removed.

Sowing & planting
Sow on edge
Handle gently
Sow indoors 

Sow one seed on edge in a 4 in. pot at about 70°F. Water as the compost begins to dry. Protect the fragile roots when moving the seedling on.

Plant in the greenhouse 

Set well-rooted plants into pots, growbags or prepared mounds once the house stays warm. Water in gently and keep water off the stem base.

Prepare a mound 

For the traditional bed method, prepare a compost-rich station about 6 in. deep and 1 ft wide.

Soil & preparation
Rich, moist, drained compost; use fresh if border soil is suspect.
Provide warm, humid air with ventilation. Avoid stagnant conditions and cold, sodden roots.
Looking after the crop
Train up a string or cane. Stop or turn the leader at the roof. Prune sideshoots for the variety, allowing one or two upper shoots to trail if space permits.
Water steadily and shade in intense heat. Dampen paths for humidity without soaking roots; ventilate to limit mould.
Female flowers have a tiny cucumber behind the petals; males have just a thin stalk. Remove male flowers for unpollinated fruit, even on all-female types. Keep them if pollination is needed: check the packet. Give regular organic liquid feed as fruit swells.
Harvesting & storage
Cut fruit before it yellows and the seeds harden. Picking often encourages new cucumbers.
Inspect daily in heat. Discard unusually bitter fruit. Trimming or cooking it is unreliable.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Red spider mite	Speckled leaves; fine webbing beneath.	Check leaf undersides; introduce suitable predators early.
Bitterness	Unusually bitter fruit.	Discard it; keep growth steady and follow flower guidance.
Mildew	White powder on older leaves.	Ventilate; keep roots moist and remove badly affected leaves.
Lack of warmth	Slow, weak growth in cold conditions.	Wait for warmth; avoid cold, waterlogged compost.
Stem and fruit rots	Grey mould or soft stem/fruit decay.	Remove infected tissue; ventilate and avoid waterlogging.
Cucumber mosaic virus	Mottled, puckered leaves; stunted growth.	Remove plants and weeds. Wash hands and tools.
Root rot	Wilting; dark, decaying roots.	Remove collapsed plants; improve drainage and avoid cold wet roots.
Final tips

Check leaf backs often; use biological mite controls early.

Support growth before it gets heavy; handle soft stems gently.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 117–121 · Growing Techniques 149–150
49
